subtopic_detail: Storage symptoms in a midlife woman and the sequence of conservative and drug treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54 year old woman who has been rushing to the toilet for the past eight months and has twice not made it in time. She passes urine about ten times a day and wakes twice at night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She drinks four cups of coffee and two cups of tea daily and has cut her water intake right down to try to control the problem. Her last period was three years ago and she takes no medication. Pelvic examination shows well oestrogenised vaginal skin with no prolapse beyond the hymen and a good pelvic floor contraction, and her post void residual measured on bladder scan is 30 mL.

data_table.Examination: No prolapse beyond the hymen, no leakage on cough with a full bladder, good voluntary pelvic floor contraction, post void residual 30 mL
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy and culture no growth; fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); bladder diary shows 10 daytime voids and 2 nocturnal voids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy follows a trial of conservative measures, and oxybutynin in particular carries the highest anticholinergic burden of the class with dry mouth, constipation and cognitive effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology; RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Refer for a mid urethral sling procedure on the gynaecology waiting list
options.rationale: A sling supports the urethra during rises in abdominal pressure and treats stress leakage, and she does not leak on coughing or lifting (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before deciding on any further treatment
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for mixed or unclear pictures, previous surgery or planned surgery, and it does not change management in a woman with clear storage symptoms and a normal residual (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream three nights a week for three months
options.rationale: Local oestrogen helps when there is genitourinary atrophy contributing to urgency, and her vaginal skin is well oestrogenised on examination (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Start bladder training with caffeine reduction and normalised fluid intake
options.rationale: Bladder retraining with timed voiding, urge suppression, reduction of caffeine and correction of fluid restriction is the recommended first step for storage symptoms and cures or improves a large proportion of women before any drug is needed (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence; Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology).

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom diagnosis of urgency with or without urgency incontinence, usually with frequency and nocturia, once infection, glycosuria and incomplete emptying have been excluded. The bladder diary does most of the diagnostic work and also reveals the two self imposed aggravators seen here: heavy caffeine intake and paradoxical fluid restriction, which concentrates urine and worsens urgency. Conservative treatment over six to twelve weeks is effective and free of adverse effects, so it precedes drug therapy. When medication is needed, a beta 3 agonist or a more selective antimuscarinic is preferred over oxybutynin, particularly in older women where anticholinergic load matters.
key_points: Exclude infection, diabetes and incomplete emptying before labelling storage symptoms
A three day bladder diary guides both diagnosis and behavioural treatment
Fluid restriction concentrates urine and worsens urgency
Bladder training precedes drug therapy and works in a large proportion of women
Oxybutynin carries the highest anticholinergic burden of the class
explanation.pearls: Caffeine above about 200 mg daily measurably worsens urgency, so cutting six caffeinated drinks to two while restoring normal water intake is a specific instruction that outperforms a vague advice to drink less.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding with a focal endometrial abnormality on transvaginal ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the outpatient clinic. A 58 year old woman was referred after two episodes of light vaginal bleeding, six years after her last period. She has never used menopausal hormone therapy and has a body mass index of 34 kg per square metre.

Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and no blood in the vault today. Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 11 mm with a discrete echogenic lesion 14 mm across within the cavity, which has a single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, and normal ovaries.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, mobile non tender uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness 11 mm with a 14 mm intracavity echogenic lesion and a single feeding vessel, normal ovaries, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and removal of the lesion
options.rationale: A focal lesion needs to be seen and removed under direct vision, because a blind sampling device can pass alongside a polyp and return a reassuring result while the abnormal tissue remains in the cavity (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Perform an office endometrial pipelle biopsy and act on the histology
options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling performs well for diffuse endometrial disease but samples only a fraction of the cavity, so it is the wrong instrument once a focal lesion has been demonstrated (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Reassure her and repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months
options.rationale: Repeat imaging without tissue would be defensible only with a thin regular endometrium under 4 mm and no focal lesion, which is not what this scan shows (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Measure serum CA125 and arrange computed tomography of the abdomen
options.rationale: Tumour markers and cross sectional imaging belong to the staging of a proven cancer or the assessment of an adnexal mass, and her ovaries are normal (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Start cyclical oral progestogen and review her bleeding in three months
options.rationale: Progestogen treats confirmed hyperplasia without atypia after tissue diagnosis, and giving it first masks bleeding while leaving a possible carcinoma undiagnosed (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma, and the assessment is structured around the ultrasound. A uniformly thin endometrium at or below 4 mm has a high negative predictive value and can justify observation for a single episode, while a thickened or focally abnormal endometrium requires tissue. The instrument is chosen by the pattern: blind sampling for diffuse thickening, hysteroscopy for a focal lesion. Obesity is the dominant modifiable risk factor through peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen, and recurrent bleeding after a negative sample always warrants re-evaluation rather than reassurance.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding carries about a 10 per cent risk of endometrial cancer
An endometrial thickness at or below 4 mm has high negative predictive value
Focal lesions require hysteroscopic assessment rather than blind sampling
Obesity raises endometrial cancer risk through peripheral oestrogen production
Recurrent bleeding after a benign sample needs repeat assessment
explanation.pearls: A blind pipelle misses a meaningful proportion of focal lesions such as polyps and localised carcinoma, so a benign pipelle result in a woman whose scan showed a discrete intracavity lesion does not close the episode.

subtopic_detail: Severe oligozoospermia on a first semen analysis and the workup it triggers
stem:
You are the doctor in a fertility clinic seeing a couple who have been trying to conceive for 14 months with intercourse every two to three days. The woman is 29 with regular 29 day cycles, a normal pelvic ultrasound, an anti-Mullerian hormone in the expected range for her age, and patent tubes on hysterosalpingogram.

Her 32 year old partner has fathered no previous pregnancies. He is well, takes no medication and does not use anabolic steroids. His testes are of normal volume with no varicocele and both vasa are palpable. His first semen analysis, produced after three days of abstinence, is shown below and he has not previously had one.

data_table.Examination: Normal secondary sexual characteristics, testicular volume 18 mL bilaterally, both vasa palpable, no varicocele
data_table.Investigations: Semen volume 2.8 mL; sperm concentration 4 x10^6 per mL; progressive motility 20 per cent; normal morphology 2 per cent; no antisperm antibodies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to intrauterine insemination in her next ovulatory cycle now
options.rationale: Insemination depends on an adequate total motile count after preparation, and success rates fall away at the concentration seen here (Source: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Repeat the analysis in three months with testosterone, FSH and LH levels
options.rationale: A single abnormal result is confirmed on a repeat sample after a full spermatogenic cycle of about 72 days, and a concentration this low triggers endocrine assessment to separate primary testicular failure from a hypothalamic pituitary cause (Source: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand; RACGP Male Infertility).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Refer directly for intracytoplasmic sperm injection using this sample
options.rationale: Injection is likely to be needed eventually, but committing before confirmation skips the karyotype and Y chromosome microdeletion testing that changes counselling about a son inheriting the defect (Source: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Prescribe clomiphene for him and reassess his semen in three months time
options.rationale: Off label clomiphene is used in selected men with proven hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, so it cannot be chosen before the gonadotropins have been measured (Source: RACGP Male Infertility).

options.text: Advise another 12 months of timed intercourse before further assessment
options.rationale: Investigation is indicated after 12 months of unprotected intercourse, and this couple has already crossed that threshold with a demonstrated abnormality (Source: RACGP Male Infertility).

explanation.summary: A male factor contributes to about half of couples presenting with infertility, and semen analysis is the single most informative test, but it is also biologically variable between samples. Because spermatogenesis takes approximately 72 days, a repeat sample is taken after an interval that reflects a full cycle rather than a fortnight later. A concentration below 5 million per mL is the accepted threshold for karyotype and Y chromosome microdeletion testing, since chromosomal causes are found in a meaningful minority and are transmissible to male offspring through injection techniques. Gonadotropins and testosterone separate primary testicular failure, which shows a high follicle stimulating hormone, from the rarer treatable central causes.
key_points: Confirm an abnormal semen analysis on a repeat sample after about three months
A raised follicle stimulating hormone points to primary testicular failure
Concentration below 5 million per mL prompts karyotype and Y microdeletion testing
Intrauterine insemination depends on the total motile count after preparation
Genetic results change counselling before intracytoplasmic sperm injection
explanation.pearls: Spermatogenesis takes about 72 days, so a repeat semen analysis is scheduled at three months rather than at three weeks, and a febrile illness in the preceding two months is enough to explain a transiently poor result.

sources.label: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea and a uterus present on imaging
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 15 year old girl brought by her mother because she has never had a period, and for the last eight months has had lower abdominal pain that lasts three or four days and comes at roughly monthly intervals.

Her breast development and pubic hair are fully developed and her growth has followed the 50th centile. She has no cyclical nasal or urinary symptoms. On examination her abdomen is soft with a tender suprapubic mass palpable two finger breadths above the pubic symphysis. Inspection of the introitus shows a normal hymenal opening with no bulging blue membrane, and a gentle cotton bud examination meets a smooth blind end after about 3 cm. Ultrasound reports a uterus containing echogenic fluid, both ovaries normal, and both kidneys present.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, tender suprapubic mass, normal hymenal opening, vagina ending blindly at about 3 cm
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus distended with echogenic fluid, normal ovaries and two normal kidneys

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Incise the membrane at the introitus under local anaesthetic in clinic
options.rationale: A simple incision drains an imperforate hymen, which presents with a bulging blue membrane at a normal introitus, and blind incision of a higher obstruction risks injury to bladder and rectum (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea; RCH CPG: Gynaecology).

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone before any further imaging
options.rationale: Androgen insensitivity is characterised by absent or sparse pubic hair with no uterus, and a uterus filled with menstrual blood excludes it (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea).

options.text: Start a continuous combined oral contraceptive to suppress her cycles
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression relieves the pain temporarily but leaves obstructed blood in the uterus and tubes, with retrograde spill and endometriosis as the consequence (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea).

options.text: Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging and refer to a specialist unit
options.rationale: With a uterus present and a blind ending vagina the obstruction lies above the hymen, and imaging is needed to define the level, thickness and any associated anomaly before a single definitive operation is planned (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea; RCH CPG: Gynaecology).

options.text: Book diagnostic laparoscopy to inspect the pelvis and drain the uterus
options.rationale: Laparoscopy assesses the peritoneal cavity but does not define the vaginal anatomy that determines the surgical approach, and it is not the first investigation (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea).

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics and cyclical pain points to an outflow obstruction rather than to an endocrine cause, because the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis is clearly working. The examination separates the two levels: a bulging blue membrane at a normal introitus is an imperforate hymen, while a normal hymen with a short blind ending vagina indicates a transverse septum or vaginal agenesis higher up. Magnetic resonance imaging defines the thickness of the obstructing segment and the length of the upper vagina, both of which dictate the operation and the likelihood of needing graft reconstruction. These procedures belong in a unit with paediatric and adolescent gynaecology experience, because a poorly planned first operation creates stenosis that is difficult to salvage.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain suggests obstruction, not endocrine failure
A bulging blue membrane means imperforate hymen and simple incision
A normal hymen with a blind vagina means a higher obstruction needing imaging
A uterus present on imaging excludes androgen insensitivity
Renal tract anomalies commonly accompany Mullerian anomalies
explanation.pearls: A transverse vaginal septum thicker than about 1 cm on magnetic resonance imaging predicts the need for graft or flap reconstruction rather than simple excision, which is why the scan precedes the knife.

subtopic_detail: Median nerve symptoms in the third trimester with motor signs
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic seeing a 33 year old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy who has had pins and needles in both hands for six weeks. It began at night and woke her, and she used to relieve it by hanging her hand out of the bed.

For the past fortnight the numbness in the right thumb, index and middle fingers has been constant rather than intermittent, and she has dropped her cup twice and cannot fasten her bra. Her blood pressure is 110/70 with no proteinuria and her ankles are only mildly swollen. On the right, thumb abduction is weak against resistance and there is early flattening of the thenar eminence. Sensation over the thenar skin itself is preserved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7, foetal heart rate 145
data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation over the right thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar skin, weak thumb abduction, early thenar wasting, symmetrical reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick no protein; thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fit night wrist splints and reassure her that it settles after delivery
options.rationale: Splinting with reassurance is right while symptoms are sensory and intermittent, but established weakness with wasting will not reliably recover if treatment waits for delivery (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; RANZCOG Common Problems in Pregnancy).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for two weeks and review her hands in the clinic
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid gives short lived symptomatic benefit only and does not decompress a nerve that is already showing motor loss (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies and urgent hand surgical assessment
options.rationale: Motor weakness with thenar wasting is the red flag that converts expectant management into assessment for decompression, and studies quantify the block and confirm the lesion is at the wrist (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; RANZCOG Common Problems in Pregnancy).

options.text: Take preeclampsia bloods and arrange review in the day assessment unit
options.rationale: Generalised oedema from preeclampsia can precipitate median nerve compression, but a normal blood pressure with no proteinuria makes that diagnosis untenable here (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange cervical spine imaging after delivery for a possible radiculopathy
options.rationale: A C6 radiculopathy produces neck and radiating arm pain with an altered reflex and sensory loss over the thenar skin, and thenar sensation is spared here because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist affects a substantial minority of pregnant women, driven by fluid retention in the third trimester, and the great majority resolve within weeks to months of delivery. That benign natural history creates the anti-pattern: symptoms are attributed to pregnancy and the examination that would detect motor involvement is not performed. Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence is the anatomical clue that the lesion sits at the wrist rather than in the neck, since the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum. Persistent numbness with weakness and wasting predicts incomplete recovery and warrants surgical assessment rather than waiting.
key_points: Most pregnancy related carpal tunnel syndrome resolves within months of delivery
Test thumb abduction strength and look for thenar wasting at every review
Preserved thenar skin sensation localises the lesion to the wrist
Night splints are first line while symptoms remain sensory and intermittent
Weakness or wasting warrants nerve conduction studies and surgical review
explanation.pearls: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves proximal to the flexor retinaculum, so numbness that includes the thenar skin points away from the carpal tunnel and towards a C6 root lesion.
